utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Let me first make sure that everybody can hear me. Mr. Mrdja, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-02-59-I, the Prosecutor versus Darko Mrjda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And may we have the appearances. First of all, Mr. Koumjian for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Nicholas Koumjian, assisted by Gina Butler for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Tom Moran for the Defence for the purposes of this hearing only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moran, did you receive the necessary documents in preparation of this initial appearance?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Were you able to discuss the issue with your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. At this point, let me turn to Mr. Mrdja who is appearing today on the basis of the indictment of April 16, 2002. He was arrested the 13th of June. The legal basis was an arrest warrant dated 26 April, 2002. Mr. Mrdja was brought to The Hague and is, since Friday, in the United Nations Detention Unit in Scheveningen. Mr. Mrdja, would you please stand up. I should like to ask you first of all several questions. These first questions are only for the purposes of the identification, having nothing to do with the case as such. Would you please state your full name, including all first names and last names for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my name is Mrdja, Darko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is the only first name. And what about --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They call me Dado. It's easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And your father's and mother's name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my father's name is Milenko Mrdja, my mother's name is Desa Mrdja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What is the date and place of your birth?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the 28th of June, 1967. I was born in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What was your profession or occupation before you came here?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I finished metal school, training for a metal worker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's easier for you to sit down. Please sit down and give your answers whilst you're sitting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And your place of last residence, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prijedor. Do you want my exact address?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vojvode Stepo Stepanovic Street, the number is 84, Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Finally, are you married and do you have children?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am married and have two children. I have a son of seven months and a daughter of four years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mrdja. The proceedings today are your initial appearance before this Tribunal. It seems to be a formality only, but it's a very important point in time, setting, to a certain extent, the course for the entire procedure. The underlying reasons for this procedure is the following: The Prosecution has asked the Trial Chamber to confirm an indictment against you on a prima facie basis. At the same time, there was a request for an arrest warrant, forming the basis for your deprivation of liberty. Normally, the other party, in this case, you Mr. Mrdja, would have a right to be informed and heard before a decision is taken. It is in the nature of the aforementioned decisions that it was not possible to hear you beforehand. This will be cured now. You will have the possibility to contest both the indictment and the deprivation of liberty. For a better understanding of what's going on, let me give you the following informations, first of all, before reading the indictment. Mr. Mrdja, it is your right to remain silent. No inference to your disadvantage can be drawn if you remain totally silent. The only inference that can be drawn can be found in Rule 62 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence where you can read that if the accused fails to enter a plea in the initial appearance, the judge shall enter a plea of not guilty on the accused's behalf. But I have to warn you at the same time that everything you may say in the courtroom may be used even against you, in evidence. It is only fair to tell you also the other side of the same coin. It is the general rule in all courtrooms on this globe that any kind of cooperation will be or would be for your advantage. In case it will not come to a sentencing stage, it will be in your interest to speed up the proceedings. In case, and I emphasise, only in case it would come to sentencing stage, such kind of cooperation will always be held in your favour. And it's now for you to discuss this issue in depth with your Defence counsel, balancing all these interests. Mr. Mrdja, did you understand this admonition?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have understood very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now hear the charges of the indictment of April 16, without the attachment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia, pursuant to her authority under Article 18 of the statute of the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia, charges Darko Mrjda with crimes against humanity and violations of the laws or customs of war as set forth below: The accused, Darko Mrjda, nickname Dado, son of Milenko, was born on 28 June, 1968 in Zagreb, Croatia. He grew up in Tukovi, in the municipality of Prijedor in Bosnia and Herzegovina and had worked at the nearby mine in Omarska. In 1992, during the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina, he was a member of the special police unit known as an "intervention squad" serving under the Bosnian Serb authorities in Prijedor. General allegations: On 21 August, 1992, an armed conflict was taking place in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The crimes charged in this indictment were part of a widespread and systematic attack on the civilian population, principally Muslim and Croat, of Prijedor municipality. Darko Mrjda is individually criminally responsible, pursuant to article 7(1) of the statute of the Tribunal for the crimes referred to in Articles 3 and 5 of the statute of the Tribunal as alleged in this indictment, which he planned, instigated, ordered, committed or in whose planning, preparation or execution he otherwise aided and abetted. Darko Mrjda on 21 August, 1992, was required to abide by the laws and customs governing the conduct of armed conflicts including the Geneva Conventions of 1949, and the additional protocols thereto. Statement of the facts: In the spring of 1992, armed conflict broke out in the northwestern Bosnia, including the municipalities of Prijedor and Skender Vakuf. Armed forces aligned with the Serbian Democratic Party, the SDS, who sought to join the territory to the Yugoslavia or to keep it in an independent Serbian state, Republika Srpska, attacked non-Serb civilian populations and battled forces that supported the government in Sarajevo. As part of their efforts to sever territory from Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bosnian Serb forces, under the leadership of the SDS, carried out widespread and systematic attacks on the civilian population of this region. Non-Serb civilians were detained in various facilities including the Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje camps in Prijedor municipality. On 21 of August, 1992, a group of non-Serb prisoners detained in the Trnopolje camp were told that they would be "exchanged" and transported to Travnik, a city then under the control of the forces loyal to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Buses arrived at the camp that morning, and many prisoners boarded the buses. That same morning, many hundreds, or perhaps more than a thousand, civilian men, women, and children gathered in the village of Tukovi, also in Prijedor municipality. They had also been told that a convoy would be organised that day to Travnik. Darko Mrjda was present in Tukovi when the civilians were loaded on to the convoy and was observed to give orders to other police officers present. The two groups of vehicles from Tukovi and Trnopolje joined into one convoy at the town of Kozarac and proceeded in the direction of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Travnik. Police or soldiers, including Darko Mrjda, accompanied the convoy throughout the journey. After passing the town of Skender Vakuf, the convoy drove over Vlasic mountain toward the front line. At one point along the mountain road, the convoy stopped in a wooded area. Darko Mrjda was present, along with several other men in uniforms. He ordered and participated in the separation of a group of military-aged non-Serb men. The remainder of the convoy, consisting largely of women, children, and elderly, continued on to Travnik. Darko Mrjda, and a group of police from his intervention squad, ordered these non-Serb men, who had been separated, to enter two buses. There were far more men than seats, and the prisoners were packed into all available space on the buses. After driving a short distance, the buses stopped at a location called Korecanske Stijene where there is a sheer rock face on one side of the road and a steep cliff on the other. Prisoners were ordered to leave the bus with their heads down and to kneel at the edge of the cliff. Darko Mrjda said: "Here is where we do the exchange, the living for the living, and the dead..." The police began firing their guns at the men. Several jumped or were pushed over the cliff before they were shot and survived the fall. Prisoners from the other bus were then brought off the bus in smaller groups and shot at the edge of the cliff. Witnesses estimate more than 200 men were killed by the shots or the fall, although the exact number that died is unknown. Annex A lists 228 names that were reported to be those of men last seen on this convoy. 12 men are known to have survived the shooting and the fall. Darko Mrjda was in command of the police unit, planned, organised, aided, and abetted, and ordered the massacre and he himself shot at least one prisoner. Charges: On 21 August, 1992, on a road over Vlasic mountain in the municipality of Skender Vakuf, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Darko Mrjda acting in concert with others who shared his intent planned, instigated, ordered, committed, or otherwise aided and abetted the planning, preparation, or execution of the killing of over 200 men on a convoy originating from Trnopolje and Tukovi and heading for Travnik. 12 men, among those that the accused and his accomplices intended to kill, fell or jumped down a cliff and survived the massacre. By the above-described conduct, Darko Mrjda committed: Count 1: Extermination, a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5 (b) and 7(1) of the statute of the Tribunal, and count 2: Murder, a violations of the laws or customs of war as recognized by Article 31A of the Geneva Convention of 1949, punishable under Articles 3 and 7(1) of the statute of the Tribunal. Count 3: Inhuman acts, attempted murder, a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5, 1 and 7(1) of the statute of the Tribunal. Dated this 16th day of April, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As mentioned in the indictment itself, attached to the indictment we find an annex A, not to be read out here, including the names of 228 persons missing from 21 August, 1992 convoy over Vlasic Mountain. Mr. Mrdja, did you understand this indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood it, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have to inform you that under Rule 68 -- 62 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, within 30 days of this initial, you will be called upon to enter a plea of guilty or not guilty on each count; but that should you so request, you may immediately enter a plea of guilty or not guilty on one or more counts. Did you have the opportunity to discuss the charges of the indictment with your Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I discussed it in the course of the day today, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Mrdja, are you ready to enter a plea to the charges today? Are you able to tell us whether you plead guilty or not guilty to each of the counts, or would you prefer to do so within 30 days?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would prefer to do so straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then I have to ask you, what is your plea with respect to Count 1, extermination, a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5(b) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Count 2: Murder, a violation of the laws or customs of war, as recognised by Article 3(1)(a) of the Geneva Convention of 1949, punishable under Articles 3 and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And finally, Count 3: Inhumane acts, attempted murder, a crime against humanity, punishable under Articles 5(i) and 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not guilty, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you want to make any additional comments on the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You may sit down, please. Madam Registrar, we have noted that Mr. Mrdja has entered a plea of not guilty to all the counts of the indictment. We may now turn to the question of deprivation of liberty. Today I have to decide whether or not there will be ongoing deprivation of your liberty. Of course, it's your right to contest the question of your arrest. Do you want to raise any objections today, or as it is custom in this Tribunal, first to file a motion on behalf of this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we reserve and file a motion for provisional release at a later date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, then I have today to order that the detention has to continue until further order. And we expect your contributions. Is it necessary that anybody is informed on your deprivation of liberty, for example, your spouse or relative, especially to inform where you can be reached, the coordinate here in Scheveningen?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I have already contacted my family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In this context, the second question is: Do you want the Tribunal to inform your consulate or embassy on your deprivation of liberty?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if possible, I should like them to be informed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So, please, tell me, what is the consulate you want to be -- that should be informed?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The consulate of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The State of Bosnia and Herzegovina; I understand correctly. Thank you. You may be seated again. First of all --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I first of all, then, turn to the Prosecution. Any comments from the side of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my only remaining concern today is the appointment of Defence counsel, who it is that I should deliver the supporting materials to within 30 days. And I've also planned to file a motion - we can file it today - just a general protective measures motion, a standard motion in all cases, that nothing be disclosed outside of the accused and Defence counsel that could possibly endanger any witness or victim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, my client has been in contact with a lawyer I believe in Banja Luka. I have his telephone number. He will probably at least contacted to be the permanent counsel. I will also confer with the OLAD staff immediately after this hearing about the matter of permanent counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But my understanding is that for the period of transition, you will be always available as the responsible person?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I understand it, the assignment was for a few days, a limited number of days. And I would prefer not to accept service of the supporting materials if someone will be assigned in the next few days. I'd rather not have them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. I understand. But just in case it's necessary to regulate the one or other question, you will be available until new Defence counsel is arriving.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps just for the record, we should -- Your Honour may consider inquiring of the accused if he has retained a lawyer or has the funds to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I will turn immediately to this last question. Mr. Mrdja, we already mentioned the Detention Unit once again. The question is whether or not you want -- do you want to raise anything regarding the conditions of your detention and the conditions of your health?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no criticisms to make with respect to detention or anything else that I wish to say. Everything is proper and correct. And I am exceptionally happy with the conditions of detention. I have nothing to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the final question, as you may have understood from the Office of the Prosecutor: Do you have already Defence counsel which will represent your interests that you can tell the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have contacted Mr. Krstan Simic. However, he has some political reasons for which he was not able to call me back. But in a space of a day or two, I shall tell the lawyer who my Defence counsel will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. It's my understanding that both the OTP and the Trial Chamber II will be informed immediately on the ongoing developments. Any other further statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to save any time being wasted, I don't know if the accused is indicating he has funds to actually hire counsel or if he's going to request an appointment. I think OLAD may be interested in knowing that so they can start working on an appointment if that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've conferred with him. And for purposes of appointment of counsel, he is indigent, and he will claim indigence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. I think the proceedings can go on on this basis, and the Trial Chamber expects new motions from both sides as soon as possible. I can conclude this hearing. This hearing stands adjourned. Thank you all.
